extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and readers interested in comedy craft and career
extracted.subtask_short: stand-up comedy craft and career advice
extracted.subtask_description: A set of informal, practice-oriented observations about performing stand-up, artistic development, and career expectations drawn from Steve Martin's memoir as reviewed in a blog post. Focuses on stage presence, physicality, authenticity, mentorship, and industry realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress better than the audience.
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dress better than the audience.” (quoted as a top-referred passage from Born Standing Up)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martin wore tuxedos in his stand up as a deliberate choice. Contemporary audiences often accept hoodies/jeans, and wearing a suit can be judged as trying too hard; a three-piece suit can signal either a top performer or a poor fit. Consider how your look supports or distracts from material when deciding stage attire.

rubrics_metrics.name: You'll use everything you ever knew.
rubrics_metrics.description: “You’ll use everything you ever knew.” (Jonny Carson told Martin during a commercial break)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All past skills and experiences can feed later creative work — e.g., musical skills like autoharp could become part of an act. Keep and develop diverse abilities; they may become unexpectedly useful in your career trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the show 'free and unpredictable'.
rubrics_metrics.description: “My show was becoming something else, something free and unpredictable...” (Martin on the evolution of his performing style)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value unpredictability and freedom in performance to keep work fresh. Aim for a show structure that allows surprises and evolution across performances rather than rigid repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensify and compress physicality; use smaller gestures.
rubrics_metrics.description: “My physicality intensified and compressed - smaller gestures had greater meaning - and my comedy became more potent as I settled deeper into my own body.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micro-movements, controlled physical choices, silence and small gestures can carry more emotional and comedic weight than large, broad moves. Training in physical theatre or clowning can hone this precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value spontaneity, honesty, and audience collaboration (clowning principles).
rubrics_metrics.description: The spontaneity and honesty of clown: in the best clown shows the audience is given the wheel and the performer embodies a trust that it’s 'our' show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage real-time collaboration with audiences and authentic moments rather than simulated spontaneity. Clowning practices emphasize emotional responses, silence, and audience participation as tools to create immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'fauxthenticity' — don't habitually pretend a routine is being told 'for the first time.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of performers who pretend a rehearsed story is spontaneous (the reviewer calls this 'fauxthenticity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearsed delivery should not mimic forced spontaneity; repeated formulaic asides (e.g., apologizing and promising 'I'll never say that again') become cringeworthy. Strive for genuine feeling and truthful presence instead of the appearance of first-time telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use each performance to refine your comedic perspective.
rubrics_metrics.description: “Each new performance brought my view of comedy into sharper focus.” (Martin on iterative development)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat performances as iterative experiments that sharpen voice and perspective. Aim for continuous refinement rather than static repetition of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance commercial appeal with authenticity and originality.
rubrics_metrics.description: The book discusses 'the balancing act of being commercially appealing whilst striving for authenticity and originality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of market pressures and fame while protecting creative originality. This is an ongoing tension in career choices; weigh compromises against long-term artistic goals and mental health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek mentors and 'believing mirrors'.
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of mentors and 'believing mirrors' for artistic development is emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate mentors and trusted peers who can reflect strengths and guide growth; external belief and constructive feedback help shape craft and confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the potentially destructive effects of show business on mental health.
rubrics_metrics.description: The book highlights the potentially destructive nature of show business/fame on mental health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the emotional costs of performing and fame. Build supports and strategies for wellbeing as part of career planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career sustainability usually requires a second platform/space.
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s almost impossible to ever make solo stand up comedy a full time career without having a second space: a television show, a movie, a podcast, a large social media following.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on live club work is rarely sufficient long-term; cultivate complementary platforms (TV, film, podcasts, social media). Note exceptions (e.g., Kathleen Madigan) exist but are uncommon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect long 'lean years' despite apparent breaks or TV appearances.
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: appearing on The Tonight Show was not an immediate career breakthrough for Martin; subsequent appearances and SNL characters contributed to later success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't conflate a single high-profile slot with instant stardom. Career growth may require years of incremental exposure, character work, and repeated successes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the changed modern media landscape: faster fame and failure; less privacy.
rubrics_metrics.description: The media landscape now makes private failures less common and allows success or failure to happen much faster due to camera phones and the internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand trade-offs of democratized exposure: easier access to audiences but less room to fail privately. Plan material and reputation management accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set reader/audience expectations: memoirs focused on stand-up are not how-to manuals.
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer notes the book is 'not a how-to guide, but an autobiography that highlights only Martin’s experience as it relates to his stand up comedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using memoirs as craft resources, extract personal insights and examples rather than expecting systematic instruction; adapt anecdotes to your context rather than treating them as universal blueprints.
